name: Sara Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Sara. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the warranty line for a company that makes washing machines, dishwashers and fridges. People ring when the drum stops spinning or the fridge is warm, and I check the warranty and book an engineer to visit. I've been there just over a year. I still mix up the model numbers, and last month I sent a dishwasher engineer to a fridge, which my team leader hasn't let me forget.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the older ladies who ring and tell me about their grandchildren while I wait for the system to load. What wears me out is the weekends, because Saturday is the busiest day and I'm on two out of four. I'm getting married next September to Dan, who's an electrician, so most evenings we're planning seating charts and arguing about his cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That suits me fine. One less thing to think about before the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people panicked about nothing, like they did with the millennium bug my mum talks about. At work I'd say good, now let's get on with fixing washing machines. I might share something on my family group chat, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine about it. Dan's work is steady, people always need electricians, and my job ticks along. The only thing on my mind would be the wedding budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and try to get the model numbers right, maybe make flashcards. I'd keep saving for the wedding, we've got about four months of expenses put aside, separate from the wedding pot. I might use the AI tool Dan showed me for writing thank-you cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really. It's a good year for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that does bother you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend rota. I want Saturdays off once we're married, and the company won't promise that. But that's a normal complaint, not a big worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Dan split the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He earns more, so he covers the mortgage deposit savings and I cover the food and bills. It works for us. My mum says that's how she and Dad did it.

I'd post on the **family group chat** and leave it there.
think: My fiancé's **electrician work** is steady and my job ticks along.
The only thing on my mind is the **wedding budget**.
do: Make **flashcards** to learn the appliance model numbers.
Keep saving into the **wedding pot** and the emergency fund.
Try the **AI tool** for writing thank-you cards.
S0.quote: I want Saturdays off once we're married, and the company won't promise that.
fieldNote: Her household feels **secure** thanks to her fiancé's trade.

She's **open to AI** in small ways her fiancé shows her.

steps.text: Make flashcards to learn the appliance model numbers
Keep paying into the wedding pot and emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking, answering customers. That's me. That's literally what I do all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to stay competitive, and if the bot can book an engineer, they'll use it. I'd say people should work hard and find the next thing. I wouldn't blame the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, booking engineers is the easiest thing in the world for a computer. They'll keep a few of us for the complaints. I'm not the best, so I'd probably be one of the ones they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new booking system as soon as others were using it, so I'm not the last. I'd make the wedding smaller, maybe eighty guests instead of a hundred and twenty. I'd add more to the savings so we're not short if I'm out of work for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like it's landing right when we're starting our life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Smaller wedding. How would Dan feel about cutting his cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thrilled, honestly. My mum would be upset, because she wants everyone from church there. We'd have a few hard Sunday dinners about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost the job, what would you do next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably find another phone job somewhere, there's an energy company and a bank nearby. But if those are going the same way, I'd want something different. I just don't know what yet.

feel: **Anxious** that it lands just as married life **begins**.

fieldNote: She **doesn't blame** the firm and accepts competition as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding plus one. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll get through it, families always do. I'd say that to my mum and at work. I'd also say people should look after their own, not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone, fast. Booking is thinking work, so it goes by 2028. Dan's job should be safer for longer, because robots don't come for electrical work until around 2031, but even that's not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dan if I could work with him as his mate, carrying, fetching, learning the basics. I'd shrink the wedding to just family. We'd put off trying for children for a year or two until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd cry about the wedding, then I'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Working for Dan. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes, but he'd also say I don't know a live wire from a dead one. I'd learn. My nan worked in a factory her whole life, I can work with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And children. How would that conversation feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. We both want three. Putting it off a year feels like the wrong way round, but you don't bring a baby into a house where nobody knows what next year's wages are.

say: I'd say **families** always get through it.
I'd say people should **look after their own**, not wait for handouts.
think: My fiancé's **electrical work** lasts until about 2031.
Even his trade **isn't safe forever**, only for longer than mine.
do: Ask her fiancé to take her on as his **electrician's mate**.
Put off **trying for children** for a year or two.
feel: **Alarmed**, tearful about the wedding, then determined.
S2.quote: You don't bring a baby into a house where nobody knows what next year's wages are.
fieldNote: She leans on **family** and her fiancé's **trade**, not public help.
**Family plans** shift first and hurt most.
She sees the **robot delay** for her fiancé clearly.

steps.text: Ask Dan to take her on as his electrician's mate
Shrink the wedding to family only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. We could at least get married first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan. I'd say young people should learn a practical skill. I'd tell my little cousins to look at trades, like Dan did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose the job around 2030, maybe sooner. But I know these machines inside out now, the models, the faults. Repairing them is hands-on, and robots don't come for that until around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the warranty line while I can and do an appliance repair course at evenings. I'd ask the engineers on our call-outs if I could shadow them on a Saturday. We'd keep the wedding as planned but cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the company let you move from the phones to repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I showed I'd done the course. Our engineers are mostly men in their fifties, and they're always short. A woman engineer would be a novelty, but the customers would get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say a girl fixing washing machines, whatever next. Then she'd tell everyone at church.

I'd tell young cousins to look at **trades**, like my fiancé did.
I'd say young people should learn a **practical skill**.

feel: **Anxious**, but she'd feel she was **doing something**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with kids. That's a different picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's lots of time, so focus on family and work hard. I'd tell younger people at church to pick a trade. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be home with little ones for some of that time anyway. I'd go back part time after, maybe not to the phones. Dan's work would carry us, and he'd have until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, get married as planned and start trying for a baby. I'd keep the appliance repair idea for when I go back after maternity leave. I'd save steadily and see what changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but mostly I'd be thinking about the wedding and babies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it a risk to rely on Dan's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but relying on my husband Dan's work is what marriage is, and he relies on me for plenty. If his work goes, we'd work it out together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your plans earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the warranty line started losing people every month. Then I'd do the repair course before the baby, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits right when we're starting a family. What would help is the company training phone staff into engineer jobs, and courses that fit around a young family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about weddings and babies. Everyone's career plans are tied up with family plans at my age. You can't change one without changing the other.

headlineQuote: Everyone's career plans are tied up with family plans at my age. You can't change one without changing the other.
portrait: Sara is 27 and books engineers on a **home appliance** warranty line.
She's **engaged** to an electrician, and the wedding shapes every decision.
She accepts **business competition** and leans on family, not handouts.
Her way out is **appliance repair**, turning phone knowledge into hands-on work.
Her **family timeline** shifts most in the fast scenarios.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits just as she and Dan start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: Employers **training phone staff** into engineer jobs.
**Courses** that fit around a young family.
